--- title: "Building Logic:
Operators, Conditions, and Functions" subtitle: "Week 4" date: "2025-11-24" date-format: " " format: revealjs: default categories: - week04 - slides image: images/preview_w4.png --- # Recap Week 3 ## Brief Recap Week 3 {.smaller} ::: {.columns} ::: {.column} - Data frames: row-column structure ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} df <- data.frame(x = 1:3, y = c("a", "b", "c")) df ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` x y 1 1 a 2 2 b 3 3 c ``` ::: ::: - Lists: store anything ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} my_list <- list(x = 1:3, y = letters[5:1]) my_list ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` $x [1] 1 2 3 $y [1] "e" "d" "c" "b" "a" ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: {.column .fragment} ::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"} What are the outputs for following codes? ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} df$x df[[2]] df[3, ] df[, "y", drop = FALSE] df[1, 2] ``` ::: ::: {.fragment}
::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} my_list$x my_list[1] my_list["y"] my_list[[2]][3] ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: :::{.notes} list is often used to store meta data Motivation for Week 4 - Why learn operators, conditions, and functions? - Real-world examples (e.g., filtering data, automating repetitive tasks, decision-making in analysis). ::: # Operators ## Assignment and Arithmetic Operators {.smaller} ::: {.columns} ::: {.column} - Assignment operators: `<-`, `=` ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} x <- 1 x ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 1 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} y = "abc" # not recommanded y ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "abc" ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} # assign value to function’s parameter mean(x = 1:3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 2 ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: {.column .fragment} - Arithmetic operators: `+`, `-`, `*`, `/`, `^` (exponentiation), *etc*. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} 10^3 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 1000 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.fragment} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} x <- c(2, 8, 3) x - 1 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 1 7 2 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} x - 1:3 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 1 6 0 ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: {.fragment} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} y <- c(6, 4, 1) x + y ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 8 12 4 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} x * y ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 12 32 3 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} x / y ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 0.3333333 2.0000000 3.0000000 ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: ::: ## Comparison Operators {.smaller} Element-wise comparison: `>`, `<`, `>=`, `<=`, `==`, `!=`, returns logical results. ::: {.columns} ::: {.column} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} 10 > 3 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] TRUE ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} 10 >= 3 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] TRUE ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} 10 < 3 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] FALSE ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} 10 <= 3 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] FALSE ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} 10 == 3 # equal ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] FALSE ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} 10 != 3 # not equal ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] TRUE ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: {.column .fragment} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} x <- c(2, 8, 3) y <- c(6, 8, 1) x == y ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] FALSE TRUE FALSE ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} x != y ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] TRUE FALSE TRUE ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} x > y ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] FALSE FALSE TRUE ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} x <= y ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] TRUE TRUE FALSE ``` ::: ::: ::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple" .fragment} What are the expected results? - `x == 8` - `y > 1` - `a` is a vector of numbers 1 to 5, `a[a > 3]` returns? ::: ::: ::: ## Logical Operators {.smaller} Element-wise comparison: NOT (`!`), AND (`&`), OR (`|`), *etc.*, returns logical values. ::: {.columns} ::: {.column} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} !TRUE ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] FALSE ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} !FALSE ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] TRUE ``` ::: ::: ::: {.fragment} To combine two conditions A and B: | A | B | A & B | A \| B | |-------|-------|-------|--------| | TRUE | TRUE | **TRUE** | TRUE | | TRUE | FALSE | FALSE | TRUE | | FALSE | TRUE | FALSE | TRUE | | FALSE | FALSE | FALSE | **FALSE** | ::: ::: ::: {.column .fragment} ::: { .callout-tip appearance="simple"} What are the expected results? - `(3 > 1) & (7 < 5)` - `(3 > 1) | (7 < 5)` ::: ::: {.fragment} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} (3 > 1) & (7 < 5) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] FALSE ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} (3 > 1) | (7 < 5) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] TRUE ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: ::: ## The `%in%` Operator {.smaller} We use `%in%` to check if left-side values are present in right-side, it returns logical values. ::: {.columns} ::: {.column} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ## check membership 1 %in% 1:3 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] TRUE ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} 1:3 %in% 1 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] TRUE FALSE FALSE ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} "a" %in% c("abc", "a") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] TRUE ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: {.column} ::: {.fragment .callout-tip appearance="simple"} Data frame `df` has two columns named `x` and `y`, what is the result of following code? `"col3" %in% colnames(df)` ::: ::: {.fragment} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} "col3" %in% colnames(df) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] FALSE ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: :::
::: {.fragment .callout-tip appearance="simple"} If you are on R 4.6+, you can use the newly introduced `%notin%` operator to check whether a value is *not* in a collection. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} "a" %notin% c("abc", "a") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] FALSE ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} 5 %notin% 1:3 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] TRUE ``` ::: ::: ::: ## Bonus: Operator Precedence {.smaller} ::: {.columns} ::: {.column} Simplified precedence order[^1] (highest to lowest): 1. Arithmetic (`^` > `*`, `/` > `+`, `-`) 2. Relational (`>`, `<`, `>=`, `<=`, `==`, `!=`) 3. Membership (`%in%`) 4. Logical (`!` > `&` > `|`) ::: ::: {.column .fragment} Order can be change using `()`: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} 1 + 2 * 3 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 7 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} (1 + 2) * 3 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 9 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.fragment} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} TRUE | TRUE & FALSE ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] TRUE ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: {.fragment} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} (TRUE | TRUE) & FALSE ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] FALSE ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: ::: [^1]: For more detail, check the [operator documentation](https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/base/html/Syntax.html). ## `any()`, `all()` and `which()` {.smaller} ::: {.columns} ::: {.column} Given a set of logical vectors: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} -3:3 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] -3 -2 -1 0 1 2 3 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} -3:3 > 0 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE TRUE TRUE TRUE ``` ::: ::: - `any()`: is at least one of the values `TRUE`? ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} any(-3:3 > 0) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] TRUE ``` ::: ::: - `all()`: are all of the values `TRUE`? ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} all(-3:3 > 0) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] FALSE ``` ::: ::: - `which()`: return indices of `TRUE` values. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} which(-3:3 > 0) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 5 6 7 ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: {.column .fragment} ::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"} We have a vector `log2FoldChange <- c(1.2, -0.5, 0.9, 0.7, -1.1)`, what are the expected results for the following codes? - `which(log2FoldChange > 0.8)` - `any(log2FoldChange > 0.8)` - `all(log2FoldChange > 0)` ::: ::: ::: # Conditions ## Conditional Statements {.smaller} Conditional statements allow us to make decisions based on logical conditions, guiding how the code behaves in different scenarios. ```{mermaid} %%| echo: false %%| fig-width: 10 flowchart LR AA[Age] --> A(("< 18")) A --> B(TRUE) A --> C(FALSE) B --> D["print 'Minor'"] C --> E["print 'Adult'"] ``` . . . ```{mermaid} %%| echo: false %%| fig-width: 10 flowchart LR AA[P-value] --> A(("< 0.05")) A --> B(TRUE) A --> C(FALSE) B --> D["print 'Significant'"] C --> E["print 'Non significant'"] ``` ## `if` and `if else` {.smaller} ::: {.columns} ::: {.column} Syntax: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ## if statement if (condition) { # code to run if `condition` is TRUE } ## if else statement if (condition) { # code to run if `condition` is TRUE } else { # code to run if `condition` is FALSE } ``` ::: ::: {.callout-important appearance="simple"} - You can use `if` without `else` but never in the opposite way. - The condition must evaluate to exactly **one logical value** (`TRUE` or `FALSE`) and cannot be NA. ::: ::: ::: {.column .fragment} ```{mermaid} %%| echo: false flowchart LR AA[P-value] --> A(("< 0.05")) A --> B(TRUE) A --> C(FALSE) B --> D["print 'Significant'"] C --> E["print 'Non significant'"] ``` ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} pvalue <- 0.1 if (pvalue < 0.05) { # code to run if condition is TRUE print("Significant") } else { # code to run if condition is FALSE print("Non significant") } ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "Non significant" ``` ::: ::: ::: {.fragment .callout-tip appearance="simple"} What will you get when `pvalue` is 0.03? ::: ::: {.fragment} ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "Significant" ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: ::: ## The `ifelse()` Function {.smaller} Syntax: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ifelse(test, yes, no) ``` ::: Example: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} pvalue <- 0.01 ifelse(test = pvalue < 0.05, yes = "Significant", no = "Non significant") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "Significant" ``` ::: ::: . . . The "test" parameter can be a logical vector. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} vec_p <- c(0.02, 0.049, 0.1) ifelse(vec_p < 0.05, yes = "Significant", no = "Non significant") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "Significant" "Significant" "Non significant" ``` ::: ::: # Functions ## What is a Function? {.smaller} Functions = Reusable blocks of code. . . . ![](images/call_function.png) ::: {.notes} Functions that are part of R's base installation, always available without needing to load any additional packages. To use a function, write the **function's name** followed by `()`, place any required input (arguments/parameters) inside the `()`. ::: ::: {.fragment .callout-note appearance="simple"} Use `?` or `help()` to view the function's documentation, *e.g.*: `?mean`, `help(mean)` ::: ## Using Functions {.smaller} Functions = Reusable blocks of code. - Built-in functions ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} mean(x = 1:3) ``` ::: - Functions from additional packages ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # install.packages("readr") # one time only if not yet installed library(readr) # load the package (every new R session) read_csv(file = "path/to/data.csv") ``` ::: ::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"} We'll talk about packages next week! ::: . . . - Custom functions ::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"} We'll talk about customised functions in session 8! ::: # Let's Practice ! ## Today's Goals - Understand and use operators to filter data with precision. - Apply functions to perform basic calculations and data manipulation.

<script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
